en: Theravāda Vinaya Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga Pāṭidesanīyakaṇḍa (The Chapter on Offenses Requiring Confession for Nuns)
2–8. The Training Rule on Requesting Oil, Honey, Molasses, Fish, Meat, Milk, and Curd.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the group of six bhikkhunīs, having requested oil, consumed it.
...pe... they requested honey and ate it.
...pe... they requested molasses and ate it.
...pe... they requested fish and ate it.
...pe... they request meat and eat it.
...pe... they request milk and eat it.
...pe... they request curd and eat it.
People complained, grumbled, and spread it about:
"How can these bhikkhunīs request curd and then eat it?
To whom would what is excellent not be pleasing? To whom would what is delicious not be agreeable?"
The bhikkhunīs heard those people criticizing, disparaging, and complaining.
Those bhikkhunīs who were few in desires... [as before] ...criticized, disparaged, and complained:
"How can the bhikkhunīs of the group of six request curd and then eat it?"... [as before] ...
“Is it true, monks, that the group-of-six bhikkhunīs, having requested curd, eat it?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them… [as before]…
"How indeed, monks, could the group-of-six bhikkhunīs request curd and then eat it?
This, monks, is neither for the inspiration of those without faith nor for the increase of the faith of those who have faith...
And furthermore, monks, the bhikkhunīs should recite this training rule thus:"
“Whatever bhikkhunī, having requested curd, should eat it, that bhikkhunī must confess:
‘Venerable ladies, I have committed an offense that is blameworthy, unseemly, and entailing confession; I confess it.
Thus was this training rule for the bhikkhunīs laid down by the Blessed One.
Now at that time, some bhikkhunīs were ill.
The bhikkhunīs who went to inquire after their health said to those who were ill:
“We hope, noble ladies, that you are bearing up; we hope that you are getting by?”
“Previously, noble lady, we used to ask for curd and eat it, and because of that we were comfortable.
But now, fearing wrongdoing on the grounds that ‘it has been forbidden by the Blessed One,’ we do not ask for it, and because of that we are not comfortable.
… [They] reported this matter to the Blessed One … [as before].
“I allow, monks, a sick bhikkhunī to request curd and eat it.
And furthermore, monks, the bhikkhunīs should recite this training rule:
‘Whatever bhikkhunī, not being sick, [requests oil …pe…’”
Honey …pe… molasses …pe… fish …pe…
If she should request meat ... pe ... milk ... pe ...
or curd and eat it, that bhikkhunī must confess it thus:
“Venerable lady, I have committed an offense that is blameworthy, unbecoming, and one requiring confession;
I confess it. “Whoever” means whoever of such a kind… [and so forth].
"A bhikkhunī" ...
[as before] ... this is the kind of bhikkhunī intended in this context.
"Not ill" means:
One for whom there is comfort without curds.
One who is ill is one for whom there is no comfort without curds.
Oil means sesame oil,
mustard oil, madhuka oil, castor oil, or fat oil.
Honey means...
Honey from bees.
Molasses is that which is produced from sugarcane.
"Fish" is said to be a water-dweller.
"Flesh" is said to be...
Meat that is allowable is the meat of those [animals] whose meat is permitted.
Milk means cow’s milk, or goat’s milk, or buffalo’s milk; it is the milk of those [animals] whose meat is permitted.
"Curd" means curd of that very same [cow].
If one who is not ill requests it for her own sake, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in the act of requesting.
If she receives it with the thought, "I shall eat it," by the very act of receiving, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
For every mouthful swallowed, there is an offense entailing confession (pāṭidesanīya).
If one who is not ill, perceiving herself as not ill, asks for curd and eats it, there is an offense entailing confession.
If one who is not ill, being in doubt, requests curd and eats it, there is an offense entailing confession (pāṭidesanīya).
If one who is not ill, perceiving herself to be ill, requests curd and eats it, there is an offense entailing confession.
If one who is ill, perceiving herself to be not ill, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If she is ill but is in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If she is ill and perceives herself as ill, there is no offense.
There is no offense—
If she makes a request while ill, and having made the request while ill, eats while no longer ill;
or if she eats the remains of what was left over when she was ill.
[if it is] for relatives,
[if one has been] invited,
or for the sake of another;
"With her own wealth," "if she is insane," "if she is a first-offender."
The eighth training rule on offenses entailing acknowledgment is finished.
Noble ladies, the eight rules on offenses entailing acknowledgment have been recited.
Therefore, noble ladies, I ask you: [Are you pure in this matter?]
“Are you pure in this matter?
A second time I ask:
“Are you pure in this matter?”
A third time I ask:
"Are you pure in this matter?
The venerable ones are pure herein; therefore they are silent. Thus do I understand it.
The section on offenses entailing confession in the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga is concluded.
